title: Ranveer Singh Is Building a Zombie Apocalypse. The Budget Is ₹300 Crore and the Director Made Scam 1992.
excerpt: Kalyani Priyadarshan makes her Bollywood debut in Pralay, a post-apocalyptic survival thriller with AI-driven VFX that starts shooting in August
body:
The man who turned Pakistani spy thrillers into a ₹1,850 crore franchise is now pointing a camera at the end of the world. And he's spending ₹300 crore to make sure you believe every rotting second of it.

Ranveer Singh has officially locked in Pralay, a post-apocalyptic zombie thriller directed by Jai Mehta — the man who gave us the razor-sharp Scam 1992: The Harshad Mehta Story, the series that made an entire generation understand hawala transactions over dinner. The film begins shooting in August 2026, and if the early details are anything to go on, Indian cinema is about to get its first world-class apocalypse.

The pitch is devastating in its simplicity: Mumbai has turned into a zombie wasteland, and one man will do whatever it takes to save his family. Think World War Z meets I Am Legend, except the crumbling skyline is Marine Drive, not Manhattan. The original screenplay by Mehta and Vishal Kapoor puts to rest earlier rumours that the film was adapted from José Saramago's Blindness — this is a homegrown nightmare, built from scratch.

The Budget That Made Trade Sit Up Straight

At ₹300 crore, Pralay isn't just expensive — it's a statement. The production, backed by Applause Entertainment and Ranveer's own banner Ma Kasam Films, plans to merge massive physical sets with AI-driven visual effects to create a dystopian atmosphere unlike anything the Indian box office has ever processed. For context, Dhurandhar 2 — which ran away with ₹1,850 crore worldwide — was made for ₹225 crore. Pralay's budget is a 33% jump, and the ambition is exponentially larger.

The zombie genre has essentially never been attempted at scale in Hindi cinema. While Telugu and Tamil filmmakers have dabbled in horror-adjacent spectacles, nobody has tried to build a full-blown undead apocalypse with this kind of money and this level of technical aspiration. Ranveer is betting that Indian audiences are ready for it.

Enter Kalyani Priyadarshan

The casting coup that's generating the most excitement: Kalyani Priyadarshan — daughter of the legendary director Priyadarshan — has been finalised for her Bollywood debut opposite Ranveer. She's already a star in the South, with standout turns in Malayalam and Telugu cinema, but this would be her first Hindi film. The pairing is entirely unexpected, and that's exactly why it works. There's no recycled chemistry here, no audience baggage. Just two actors walking into a dead city.

For diaspora viewers who've watched Kalyani light up screens in Hridayam and Bro Daddy, seeing her step into a Hindi zombie thriller alongside Ranveer Singh is the kind of crossover that makes you lean forward.

Why Jai Mehta Is the Right Call

Jai Mehta's Scam 1992 wasn't just a hit — it was a cultural reset. The series swept 11 wins from 14 nominations at the 2021 Filmfare OTT Awards, Achint Thakkar's theme music crossed 7 million streams, and the show turned financial fraud into appointment television. Mehta proved he could take dense, complicated material and make it grip you by the throat.

A zombie film requires a different set of muscles — action, VFX, pacing, dread — but the through-line is the same: making you care desperately about people in impossible situations. If anyone can turn a man running through zombie-infested Mumbai into something that feels as urgent and human as Harshad Mehta's rise and fall, it's this director.

The Bigger Picture

Ranveer's pivot from the Don franchise to Pralay tells you everything about where his head is. After reportedly paying ₹10 crore to exit Don 3, he fast-tracked the zombie project instead — choosing risk over safety, genre-breaking over franchise repetition. With Dhurandhar 2 still fresh in the rearview and a mythological collaboration with Aditya Dhar on the horizon, he's building a filmography that refuses to repeat itself.

For NRI audiences tracking Bollywood's evolution, Pralay represents something genuinely new: an Indian film that's competing not with other Bollywood releases, but with the global genre playbook. If it lands, it changes what Indian cinema is allowed to be. If it doesn't, at least someone finally tried.

Shooting begins August 2026. Clear your calendars. Board up your windows.
